articles.title: Woman Unknown wins Venice film festival as NAZA takes special jury prize
articles.summary: May el-Toukhy becomes eighth female director to take Golden Lion as Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love and Guardian-produced exposé of Israel’s Gaza killings also awarded. Bold and bravura choices as Venice celebrates A Woman Unknown, Possible Love – and NAZA.
body: May el-Toukhy’s Woman Unknown has scooped the Golden Lion at the Venice film festival, at an awards ceremony that also saw the Gaza documentary NAZA win the jury prize.

Set in the immediate aftermath of Danish liberation from Nazi occupation, the Egyptian-Danish director’s film tells the story of a young housemaid, Marie (Mathilde Arcel), who is about to marry her widowed employer but anxious about him discovering a shameful secret in her past: during the war, Marie had an intimate relationship with a German soldier.
The Guardian’s film critic hailed Woman Unknown as “elegantly appointed” in his review, likening it to Alfred Hitchcock’s Rebecca.

Arcel also won the festival’s best actress prize, the Volpi Cup, which puzzled some critics: usually, Venice doesn’t award more than one prize to a film. Speaking to the press after the ceremony, the jury president, Maggie Gyllenhaal, said they were able to make an exception because the jury’s vote for the Danish actor was unanimous. “She is going to blow our socks off,” she said.
points: Bold and bravura choices as Venice celebrates A Woman Unknown, Possible Love – and NAZA.

articles.title: Bold and bravura choices as Venice celebrates A Woman Unknown, Possible Love – and NAZA
articles.summary: After facing heavy criticism over its lack of female directors, the film festival may have redeemed itself with its winners’ list. Woman Unknown wins Venice film festival as NAZA takes special jury prize. Did the Venice film festival just redeem itself on the sexism issue?
body: Having been pilloried for failing to include enough women film-makers, the festival awarded the Golden Lion to Woman Unknown, by the Danish-Egyptian director May el-Toukhy, her gripping and stylish drama-thriller about sexual shame, political paranoia and the return of the repressed in Denmark after the second world war.

It’s a film with an elegant twist of Hitchcock’s Rebecca. A rich factory owner and widower, who preserved his wealth by doing business with the German occupiers, now wishes to marry Marie, the nanny of his infant daughter, played by Mathilde Arcel, who has also won the Volpi Cup for best actress. But this young woman has an awful secret, which arises just as she is taking the white wedding gown of her employer’s first wife to the dressmaker to be altered so she can wear it at the ceremony at her husband’s cold insistence. A very Hitchcockian touch.
points: After facing heavy criticism over its lack of female directors, the film festival may have redeemed itself with its winners’ list.

articles.title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Premieres at TIFF: A Movie About a Best Picture Winner That’s a Best Picture Contender?
articles.summary: Yo Adrian, Rocky did it … again! Only this time, the famed character is at TIFF in biopic form, thanks to director Peter Farrelly, screenwriter Peter Gamble and a star-making turn from Anthony Ippolito, who portrays actor Sylvester Stallone in the story of his relentless determination to bring…
body: “ I Play Rocky ” held its world premiere Saturday night as part of the festival’s Special Presentations program at the Princess of Wales Theatre. It’s one of the very first movies that has played at the festival that has the potential to win TIFF’s highest honor — the People’s Choice Award. Multiple applauses rang throughout the film as the film recreates the highest points of the 1976 MGM flick that became the highest grossing movie of its respective year, went on to be nominated for 10 Oscars, and winning three including best picture. A post-screening Q&A with Farelly, Ipplolito, Stephan James, Jay Duplass and screenwriter Peter Gamble.

The film chronicles one of Hollywood’s most improbable success stories: a struggling actor with a script nobody wanted and one nonnegotiable demand — that he play the lead himself. As studios dangle money on the condition that an established star throw the punches, Stallone digs in, turning the standoff that follows into its own kind of prizefight.

articles.title: Paramount Leaving California Would Devastate Los Angeles Economy, Leaked Report Finds
articles.summary: A leaked report from the Los Angeles Economic Development Corporation outlines devastating aftershocks that would follow if David Ellison pulled Paramount Skydance out of California.
body: In August, news broke of Ellison’s plan to take Paramount Skydance out of the Golden State if California Attorney General Rob Bonta and a coalition of other state AGs did not come to the bargaining table and settle their lawsuit to stop the $111 billion merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Ellison gave the AGs until Oct. 1, or he would start packing. The company is considering states such as Georgia, Texas and Tennessee.

The report went on to outline some big-picture stats for if and when Paramount Skydance completed the move: “Once Paramount completed the entire relocation of its headquarters and other operations out of California, the state would experience the permanent loss of approximately 28,990 to 57,980 full-time jobs statewide across all industries, and losses of between $10.6 billion and $21.2 billion annually in economic output.”

On Oct. 1, Paramount Skydance will have to start paying a “ticking fee” to Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders of $7 million a day until the deal closes. The trial between Ellison and the AGs is scheduled to start on March 2, meaning that without a settlement, Paramount is on the hook for about $1.3 billion to WBD shareholders.

articles.title: ‘Everybody Wants to F— Me’ Review: Giddily Genre-Crossing Comedy Sees Right Through Taron Egerton’s Nice-Guy Act
articles.summary: Just when the victim/villain discourse about sleeper smash “Obsession” was finally beginning to die down, along comes “Everybody Wants to Fuck Me” — another story of a young man’s desires getting violently over-satisfied — to start it all up again.
body: The British star wittily holds together the swerving story impulses of Jonathan Schey's enjoyably silly battle-of-the-sexes satire, about a smooth London fuckboi who suddenly finds himself too much in demand.

It’s the poster for Agnès Varda’s feminist touchstone “Cléo from 5 to 7” on his bedroom wall that immediately raises questions about personable, clean-cut Adam (Egerton), and you can practically see them whirring through the mind of Liv (“How to Have Sex” star Mia McKenna-Bruce, in a too-brief cameo) when she wakes up in his bed one sunny Sunday morning. Great film, sure, but is he actually a fan? He might be: He’s urbane and intelligent, works as an associate in a private London gallery dedicated to showcasing female artists, and carries his things around a blue Mubi tote that will get a guffaw of recognition from any industry-adjacent audience.

articles.title: Film producer Jeremy Thomas was a cross between a kindly Cambridge don and the movie world’s cool uncle
articles.summary: The man behind The Last Emperor had the confidence of an old-fashioned studio boss along with the soul of a cineaste. To say that movie producer Jeremy Thomas was British cinema royalty did not quite do justice to his meritocratic, democratic instincts.
body: Respectively son and nephew of directors Ralph Thomas and Gerald Thomas (of Doctor in the House and Carry On fame), he was born into the industry and as an independent producer combined the confidence of an old-fashioned studio boss with the soul of a cineaste, backing his own instincts and passions, befriending film-makers and doggedly pursuing projects over years.

Thomas won a best picture Oscar for Bernardo Bertolucci’s epic The Last Emperor in 1988, a movie that gained historic western access to Beijing’s Forbidden City and which in its way perfectly reflected Jeremy’s worldview: pioneering, ambitious, intellectually curious, globalist and internationalist. He produced Jerzy Skolimowski’s The Shout in 1978 and with Skolimowski, co-produced the black comic satire Good Boy as recently as 2025. His friendships and allegiances spanned the decades and he was a vital part of European independent cinema.
points: The man behind The Last Emperor had the confidence of an old-fashioned studio boss along with the soul of a cineaste.

articles.title: Everybody Wants to F*ck Me review – Taron Egerton is hounded in sharp-toothed dating nightmare
articles.summary: Toronto film festival: It’s Get Out meets the viral Shitty Media Men list in this hugely entertaining mix of dark comedy and stalker thriller with a brilliant alternating turn from Taron Egerton. Everyone knows an Adam.
body: Everyone knows an Adam. He’s not like those other guys, the ones who won’t take no for an answer and speak lasciviously about women to their mates. He’s doing the work, listening to and uplifting female voices, working at an all-female gallery while being constantly aware of his cis white male privilege. He has a Mubi tote bag, reads Edna O’Brien’s Country Girl in Hackney cafes, has a poster of Cléo from 5 to 7 in his apartment and has even named his dog after his favourite Haim sister. He is … a nice guy.
In first-time writer-director Jonathan Schey’s canny debut Everybody Wants to Fuck Me, Adam is also a fraud.

He’s played by Taron Egerton, someone who has recently been finding his footing as an adult actor, whether as more conventional lead of Netflix’s excellent B-movie thriller Carry-On or as the less expected gonzo villain of Netflix’s mid B-movie thriller Apex. But freed from streaming shackles (he’s also led two Apple dramas, one of which I genuinely don’t think anyone knows exists), he’s able to show just how much more he can do in edgier, stranger territory and how far he’s willing to go without blinking. Turns out, pretty far.

articles.title: Oscar-winning film producer Jeremy Thomas dies aged 77
articles.summary: Best known for The Last Emperor and Sexy Beast, the British film-maker was celebrated for working with international directors throughout his decades-long career.
body: Oscar-winning producer Jeremy Thomas, whose films included The Last Emperor and Sexy Beast, has died aged 77.
The British filmmaker "passed away peacefully" surrounded by family and loved ones at his home in Oxfordshire on Friday, his publicist said in a statement.

Thomas built an international reputation over a career spanning five decades, working with directors including David Cronenberg, Nagisa Oshima, Julien Temple and Nicolas Roeg and backing independent films alongside mainstream successes.
His best known film, Bernardo Bertolucci's The Last Emperor, won nine Academy Awards, including best picture, and earned Thomas an Oscar as producer in 1988.

articles.title: Anthony Ippolito on Speaking to Sylvester Stallone Before Filming ‘I Play Rocky’: “Very Overwhelming and Daunting”
articles.summary: "It was a lot to take in because I'd spent over a year, by that point, studying him,” the actor said at THR‘s Studio at 1 Hotel during TIFF, presented by sponsor Canada Goose.
body: Anthony Ippolito, who stars as a young Sylvester Stallone in I Play Rocky, opened up about speaking with the action star in preparation for the biopic.

Ippolito revealed that he and Stallone chatted about Stallone’s early childhood and many of the difficulties he had to overcome, including paralysis of the lower left side of his face after doctors accidentally severed a nerve during childbirth. The complication gave Stallone his signature voice and look, which became famous when Rocky hit theaters in the ‘70s.

“Since he was born, he had this facial paralysis that kind of made everything difficult,” Ippolito shared. “[The paralysis] obviously made trying to become an actor really difficult. And so, hearing his firsthand account of what that is like; he really just endured a lot and went through a lot. It’s a miracle that this film came to be and that people still celebrate it 50 years later.”
Distributed by United Artists and later MGM, Rocky became one of the most financially successful sports film franchises of all time, grossing over $1.7 billion globally.
